front.title: SEcure access To Tls Local rEsources (SETTLE) Problem Statement and Requirements

abstract.t: This document defines the problem statement, common terminology, security models, and technical requirements for identifying, validating, and establishing secure connections with local network devices. It outlines the challenges of extending the Web's Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to local, offline, or "limited domain" environments. The document specifies requirements for privacy-preserving discovery, generating and distributing local trust anchors, and establishing mutually authenticated secure contexts without relying on global certificate authorities or problematic Trust On First Use (TOFU) mechanisms.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: Local networks have historically used a mix of encrypted and unencrypted communications with no common method to establish trust. Access is provided to those who have the Wi-Fi password or an Ethernet cable, and the connected device simply trusts the information provided to it by the DHCP service or Router Advertisements on that network. In contrast, the Internet increasingly uses encrypted communications with a well-regulated system of Certificate Authorities, Domain Name Providers, Address Registries, and distributed Domain Name Services that form the basis of trust on the "modern web."

With the advent of HTTPS everywhere, browsers disadvantage web services using unencrypted communications by requiring a Secure Context for features such as Direct Sockets, Geolocation, Service Workers, Web Bluetooth, WebCrypto, WebTransport, and WebRTC. The concept of "Limited Domains" encapsulates these local, constrained environments, but existing web security models struggle to adapt to them. Furthermore, modern browser security models, such as Local Network Access (LNA) , restrict public websites from making requests to private IP addresses without explicit secure contexts and user permissions.

Existing deployments of TLS on local networks typically use "self-signed" X.509 certificates that lack the endorsement of a trusted party, relying instead on Trust on First Use (TOFU) mechanisms. Because the client User Agent lacks a cryptographic trust anchor for the Infrastructure Device, it presents a "scary" certificate warning. Users frequently disregard these warnings, leading to warning fatigue and leaving them vulnerable to active interception. Conversely, network devices are unable to determine the trustworthiness of the local network, humorous solutions such as the "evil bit" from aside.

This document defines common terminology and requirements for discovering, identifying, validating, and establishing secure connections with local network devices without relying on Trust On First Use (TOFU) or continuous Internet connectivity. Importantly, nothing here will help determine whether a network or network device is actually trustworthy, merely that it possesses a verifiable identity.

section.title: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: The process of establishing an initial trust relationship and secure communication channel between a User Agent and a Device where no prior relationship exists.
A party or service that provides Cryptographic Identities that are signed by one or more Trust Anchors for the purpose of establishing trust .
A Device used primarily by End Users to access services, e.g., a smartphone, a laptop, a tablet.
A Cryptographic Identity bound to a Client Device that has been signed by a Trust Anchor.
A persistent, cryptographically verifiable identifier, e.g., an X.509 public key infrastructure certificate .
An entity with a network interface that connects to a local network.
A Cryptographic Identifier bound to a specific Device. This may be derived from a hardware manufacturer root, e.g., Initial Device Identifier, IDevID , or locally generated value.
A DNS or mDNS label for a Device.
A Device providing a service on the local network, e.g., a printer, a router, an IoT hub.
A Cryptographic Identity bound to an Infrastructure Device that has been signed by a Trust Anchor.
A Certificate Authority for the local network.
A Trust Anchor for the local network.
A program that can originate authoritative responses for a given target resource , e.g. a web server..

A mechanism for transferring trust entropy via a channel physically separate from the network. [MOVE THIS: Different mechanisms offer varying security properties, including QR codes (visual, high entropy), PIN entry (manual, low entropy), Short Authentication Strings (SAS), Near Field Communication (NFC), or Push-Button Configuration (PBC).]
Communications between two Devices whose Identities have been verified and use methods such as cryptography to protect any data from eavesdropping or undetected modification.

An Infrastructure Device that is designated as the Local Certificate Authority/trust broker, transitioning a mesh of unverified devices into a hub-and-spoke trust topology. [QUESTION: Is the latter a hard requirement or just how current referees are defined/implemented?]
An environment meeting the minimum standards of authentication and confidentiality as defined by the W3C Secure Contexts specification .
A Cryptographic Identity that is trusted by a Client Device and/or UA.

An approach where a Client Device and/or UA accepts the first Cryptographic Identity presented by an Infrastructure Device or Origin Server. The identity is sometimes confirmed by an End User before acceptance.
A client program that initiates a request to an Origin Server , e.g., a web browser.

section.title: Overview and Goals
section.t: SEcure access To Tls Local rEsources (SETTLE) is concerned with enabling Protected Communications within any Zero-Trust Local Area Network. Protected Communications typically are implemented using TLS with X.509 certificates signed by a known Trust Anchor. Importantly, SETTLE does not deal with the notion of trustworthiness (authentication, authorization, access control, and/or attestation) or Users but instead is focused on the more basic issues of Device Identity verification and the use of a Local Certificate Authority and Trust Anchor to permit local autonomous operation without an active connection to the Internet.
The goals of SETTLE include:

ul.li: Autonomous/Semi-Autonomous Operation: Allow Devices to connect and obtain credentials automatically whenever possible.
Common Connection/Policy Support:: Make it possible for Devices to better adapt and participate on LANs with different capabilities and/or policies, particularly home vs. enterprise networks.
Improved Security: Eliminate the use of TOFU policies for IoT Devices by using X.509 certificates that are signed by a Local Trust Anchor.
Improved User Experience: Enable normal HTTPS access to Devices such as cameras, printers, routers, etc. using a standard User Agent such as a web browser.
Standalone Operation: Do not require an Internet connection to function. Obviously there could be cloud/distributed/managed solutions but the core architecture/protocols do not require it.

section.t: Once a User Agent trusts a Device, the Device should be reachable through existing application protocols, such as HTTPS and WebTransport , using their normal server authentication. Applications should not need protocol-specific exceptions or a separate trust establishment step for each protocol.

dl.dd: SETTLE MUST provide a mechanism to assign unique Device Names. A Device Name MUST be unique within its discovery scope, such as the local link, and SHOULD be globally unique. Independently administered networks may still reuse a name; SETTLE MUST ensure that such a collision does not let one Device impersonate another or undermine trust relationships already established. To prevent collisions, names SHOULD incorporate high-entropy device-specific data, such as MAC addresses or public key hashes .

Device Names MUST utilize standardized namespaces reserved for local or non-DNS use to ensure broad client support. Valid namespaces include ".local" for mDNS , "home.arpa." for unicast DNS , or ".alt" .
Device Name resolution MUST NOT depend on the availability of global DNS infrastructure.

SETTLE MUST utilize standard local discovery protocols, such as DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) , Unicast Local Discovery (ULD) , or Captive Portal APIs , to locate Devices prior to authentication. Discovery records MAY carry transport-security parameters such as a certificate fingerprint , but these are unauthenticated hints and MUST NOT be treated as a Trust Anchor distribution channel (REQ-VERIFY-01).

The discovery mechanism MUST prevent passive tracking of Devices or Users. SETTLE MUST NOT broadcast static identifiers (like MAC addresses or static account hashes) in plaintext if the Device is portable. SETTLE SHOULD utilize rotating identifiers or cryptographic mechanisms like Private Set Intersection (PSI). See for an analysis of discovery privacy requirements.
SETTLE MUST NOT rely on automatic Trust On First Use (TOFU) executed exclusively over the local network interface for initial authentication.

SETTLE MUST define or profile an OOB mechanism to transfer verification entropy when a suitable Device Identity is not available. OOB material that directly authenticates a key, such as a key hash in a QR code, MUST provide at least 128 bits of entropy to resist offline attacks. OOB material consumed by a PAKE or a commit-and-compare ceremony, such as a PIN or a Short Authentication String, MAY carry less, provided the protocol limits an attacker to a bounded number of online guesses and prevents offline testing against recorded traffic .

SETTLE SHOULD support the use of manufacturer-installed certificates (e.g., IDevID , ). When used, SETTLE MUST define a mechanism (e.g., Vouchers ) to cryptographically bind the manufacturer-provided identity to the user-facing Device Name.

User Agents MUST support a Local Trust Anchor. Depending on the trust store, a locally installed WebPKI trust anchor can confer authority over any DNS name. A Local Trust Anchor MUST instead be limited to the local namespaces of REQ-NAME-02, and the User Agent MUST enforce that limit itself, since path validation may ignore name constraints carried in a self-signed trust anchor .
All communications requiring a secure context MUST utilize TLS 1.3 or equivalent modern transport security protocols.
To minimize downgrade attacks, the system SHOULD utilize Implicit TLS (connect-then-handshake) rather than connection-upgrade mechanisms (e.g., STARTTLS) .
Device certificates MUST populate the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension. User Agents MUST verify these identities in accordance with and IoT TLS profiles .

SETTLE MUST work within browser Local Network Access (LNA) policies . Devices MUST be able to serve certificates that validate under SETTLE's trust model, so that a connection permitted under LNA also yields a Secure Context. SETTLE SHOULD make the trust it establishes available to User Agents as an input to LNA decisions, so that browsers can reduce redundant prompts for Devices the User has already verified, without weakening LNA's protection against unauthorized origins.

SETTLE MUST support cryptographic agility to accommodate future algorithm deprecations, including the transition to post-quantum cryptography, and ensure interoperability between independent vendor implementations. The transition also affects the OOB Ceremony (REQ-VERIFY-02): post-quantum public keys are too large to carry conveniently in a QR code, and PAKEs in current use, such as SPAKE2 , rely on the discrete logarithm problem.
SETTLE MUST operate securely without requiring Internet connectivity.
SETTLE MUST support a hierarchical local trust model where a mutually authenticated Referee can issue credentials to Devices.
dl.dt: REQ-ARCH-03: Device Lifecycle and Key Rotation
dl.dd: SETTLE MUST provide mechanisms for routine key rotation, certificate renewal without user intervention, and trust revocation. A factory reset of a Device MUST erase the private keys, credentials, and trust bindings from its prior enrollment, other than a manufacturer-installed identity. A reset cannot remove trust bindings held by other Devices, only make them obsolete, so SETTLE MUST define how those Devices handle an obsolete binding, including when they were offline at the time of the reset.

section.title: Evil Twin and Network Impersonation
section.t: An attacker may clone a local Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin), spoof BSSIDs, or poison mDNS caches to redirect traffic to a malicious endpoint. Because SETTLE mandates an OOB Ceremony (REQ-VERIFY-02) and rejects pure TOFU, the UA will detect the certificate mismatch and abort the connection, neutralizing the impersonation.

section.title: Compromise of the Referee
section.t: The Referee acts as the root of trust for the local network. If the Referee is compromised, the attacker can issue trusted certificates for any name within the local namespace, enabling widespread MITM attacks against the UA. Clients SHOULD scope Referee trust to the explicit local namespace.

section.title: Social Engineering and Support Scams
section.t: If installing trust anchors is made significantly easier, malicious actors (e.g., fake "customer support") may instruct users to scan a malicious QR code, thereby installing a rogue trust anchor. UAs MUST provide clear, unambiguous UI warnings during the OOB ceremony about the implications of trusting a new device or Referee.

section.title: Confused Deputy Attacks
section.t: Public websites often attempt to use the browser as a "confused deputy" to attack local network devices via Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). Local Network Access (REQ-TRANS-04) addresses this directly by requiring the User's permission before a public site can reach the local network. Verifying a Client Identity complements it, letting a Device also reject permitted requests that are not authenticated.

section.title: Factory Reset Incompleteness
section.t: Research into IoT protocols has shown that hardware factory resets frequently fail to clear all administrative fabrics or ACLs, leaving devices vulnerable to prior owners. REQ-ARCH-03 mandates that a factory reset MUST completely destroy all cryptographic material linking the device to prior local trust domains.

section.title: Supply Chain Attacks
section.t: When utilizing Pre-Installed Trust (IDevID), a compromised manufacturer or stolen batch of private keys allows an attacker to masquerade as a legitimate device. UAs SHOULD support mechanisms to constrain manufacturer trust to specific scopes or require secondary local validation. Manufacturer Usage Description can bound what a compromised Device may reach once joined, but does not help establish trust.

section.title: Denial of Service
section.t: Local networks are vulnerable to resource exhaustion. Malicious peers may flood the network with mDNS advertisements, initiate thousands of TLS handshakes, or attempt to exhaust certificate enrollment limits (e.g., attacking a local ACME server). Implementations SHOULD employ rate-limiting and prioritize OOB-authenticated traffic. Carrying handshake material over multicast discovery amplifies this, since every listener on the link must parse each unsolicited flight.

section.title: Privacy Considerations
section.t: In accordance with , privacy vulnerabilities in local networks must be considered.

Device Tracking: Utilizing MAC addresses or static hardware identifiers in Local Device Names (e.g., mDNS broadcasts) allows passive observers on the local network to track device presence and infer user behavior. Portable devices SHOULD utilize privacy-preserving, rotating identifiers.

Account-Scoped Identifiers: Embedding account-level UUIDs into local certificates (as seen in some proprietary local sharing protocols) allows devices belonging to the same user to be correlated by passive observers. Device identities MUST be scoped to the device itself, not a global user account, unless protected by an encrypted transport.

Hash-Based Contact Leaks: Transmitting truncated hashes of contact information (e.g., phone numbers or emails) for mutual discovery is vulnerable to brute-force reversal. Implementations prioritizing privacy SHOULD utilize Private Set Intersection (PSI) or similar cryptographic techniques for discovery.

Discovery-Channel Metadata: Anything in a discovery record is readable by every listener on the link. A certificate fingerprint advertised in a TXT record or SVCB parameter is a stable identifier and defeats the rotating identifiers REQ-NAME-05 asks of portable Devices. Handshake material carried on the discovery channel reveals that a pairing attempt is under way even when encrypted, and its length can identify the service sought, which is why pads it to a fixed size.

section.title: Prior Art and Related Work
section.t: The SETTLE architecture builds upon and differentiates itself from several existing approaches:

ul.li: BRSKI and BRSKI-PRM: Bootstrapping Remote Secure Key Infrastructure automates provisioning using manufacturer IDevIDs. BRSKI-PRM demonstrates the value of object security (signed Vouchers) over transport security for environments where pledges cannot initiate TLS connections. While powerful, BRSKI requires a supply chain root of trust, which is absent in self-hosted consumer scenarios.

Matter Protocol: Matter utilizes Password-Authenticated Session Establishment (PASE) , built on SPAKE2+ , for onboarding with a 27-bit passcode. A PAKE tolerates a low-entropy passcode when an attacker is limited to online guesses; the flaws reported by security analyses lie in the handling, notably static salts, rather than in the passcode length itself.

Wi-Fi Easy Connect (DPP): Uses QR codes containing public keys to bootstrap WPA3 credentials . This provides a strong precedent for OOB ceremonies, though it targets network-layer access rather than application-layer TLS identity.

Open Screen Protocol: The W3C Open Screen Network Protocol provides a particularly clean construction for local device pairing without pre-shared keys. Devices establish a provisional QUIC/TLS connection using self-signed certificates, then authenticate it via SPAKE2 bound to a user-transferred PIN. This pattern of "connect first, authenticate via PAKE second" is directly applicable to SETTLE's Track A. Emerging IETF work on integrating PAKEs directly into TLS 1.3 may provide a standardized transport for this class of bootstrapping.

AirDrop / PrivateDrop: Traditional local discovery using truncated hashes leaks user identifiers. Research into Private Set Intersection (PSI) demonstrates that privacy-preserving mutual discovery is feasible with sub-second latency.

SDSI/SPKI: Simple Distributed Security Infrastructure proposed a decentralized PKI binding authorizations directly to keys. While conceptually aligned with local trust, modern web browsers mandate X.509 for compatibility.
Local Public Key Hashes: Approaches that embed public key hashes into local domain names offer self-certifying namespaces but sacrifice human-readability.

Private DNS-SD: sets out privacy requirements for service discovery. met them by multicasting a ClientHello whose Encrypted SNI is keyed to a per-service Discovery Key, so only a peer already holding that key can learn the service is present. The draft expired and left key provisioning out of scope, which is the gap an OOB Ceremony fills. A DTLS handshake carried in DNS-SD TXT record updates has since been implemented (disclosure: one editor maintains that project).

Security Parameters in Discovery Records: advertises a certificate fingerprint or Authentication Domain Name in TXT keys or SVCB parameters , and tells clients not to trust a discovered service automatically.

DANE and SSHFP: and publish a certificate or key fingerprint in DNS instead of relying on a CA. Both need DNSSEC to protect that record, and a local namespace has no signed parent, so SSHFP in practice falls back to TOFU.

Opportunistic Security: treats unauthenticated encryption and stored TOFU state as better than nothing where authentication is impossible. On a local network the User is usually present, so an OOB Ceremony is available and REQ-VERIFY-01 asks for it.
EAP-NOOB: bootstraps a device with no credentials using a user-assisted OOB message generated per ceremony, and rejects static printed codes because they can leak and be reused.

WebTransport Certificate Hashes: Browsers accept a self-signed certificate from a local server when its SHA-256 hash is supplied out of band, limited to ECDSA keys and 14 days validity . This is the extent of CA-free local TLS in a browser today. The page still has to obtain the hash through a channel it already trusts, and the hash authenticates only that WebTransport session: it does not give the User Agent trust in the Device that ordinary HTTPS or other protocols can reuse.

Local Referees and ACME: Architectures utilizing a central local hub to authenticate servers or issue certificates via a local ACME server optimize UX but require initial bootstrapping of the Referee itself.
